title: Bash Script Safety: Strict Mode to Shipping
summary: A dense field guide to writing Bash scripts that fail loudly instead of silently — strict mode, quoting, shellcheck, safe temp files, traps, idempotency, and the classic footguns that destroy data. Every chapter is a page of rules, mechanics, and copy-paste patterns.

chapters.title: Why Bash Scripts Betray You
points: Bash default is 'keep going no matter what' — a failed command sets $? but the script marches on to the next line
Failure model: every command returns an exit status; 0 = success, 1-255 = failure; only 0 is truthy in Bash's inverted logic
Silent failure example: `cd /nonexistent; rm -rf *` deletes the current directory instead of the target — the classic data-loss bug
Bash is a string language, not a data language: everything is text, splitting and globbing happen after expansion
The three expansion hazards: word splitting (IFS), pathname expansion (globbing), and empty-string collapse
Scripts get run in contexts you never tested: cron (no PATH, no TTY), CI (different shell), sudo (different HOME), Docker (dash not bash)
`#!/bin/sh` is NOT bash on Debian/Ubuntu — it's dash; arrays, `[[ ]]`, and `local` silently break
Use `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for portability over `#!/bin/bash` (bash lives in /opt or /usr/local on macOS Homebrew and NixOS)
Exit status of a pipeline is the LAST command's status by default — `grep x file | head` hides grep's failure
Interactive Bash vs script Bash differ: no aliases by default, no history expansion, different shopt defaults
Rule of thumb: if the script touches files, credentials, or production, it needs strict mode + shellcheck before it runs once
When to stop using Bash: nested data structures, arithmetic beyond integers, JSON, or >300 lines — switch to Python
Bash is still right for: process orchestration, pipes, file globs, and gluing CLI tools — the shell's native strengths
Test the failure path, not the happy path: run your script with a missing file, a full disk, and a wrong permission before trusting it

chapters.title: Strict Mode: set -euo pipefail
points: The canonical header: `set -euo pipefail` plus `IFS=$'\n\t'` — four changes that turn silence into loud failure
`set -e` (errexit): exit immediately when a command returns non-zero — turns 'keep going' into 'stop now'
`set -u` (nounset): reference an unset variable and the script dies instead of expanding to empty string
`set -o pipefail`: pipeline returns the rightmost non-zero status, so `grep x f | head` no longer hides grep's failure
`IFS=$'\n\t'`: drop space from the field separator so unquoted expansion splits on newlines/tabs only, not spaces in filenames
Write it as one line at the top, after the shebang, before any logic: `set -euo pipefail`
`set -x` (xtrace) for debugging: prints each command after expansion, prefixed with $PS4; turn off with `set +x`
Better trace prefix: `PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '` gives file, line, and function on every traced line
`set -E` (errtrace) makes ERR traps fire inside functions, subshells, and command substitutions — needed for real error handlers
Long-form names are self-documenting: `set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail`
`shopt -s inherit_errexit` (bash 4.4+) propagates errexit into command substitutions — without it `x=$(false; echo hi)` succeeds
`shopt -s failglob` errors when a glob matches nothing; `shopt -s nullglob` expands it to nothing instead of the literal pattern
Check version before relying on modern features: `((BASH_VERSINFO[0] >= 4)) || { echo 'need bash 4+' >&2; exit 1; }` — macOS ships bash 3.2 (GPLv2)
Strict mode is a floor, not a ceiling: it catches typos and missing files, not logic errors or race conditions

chapters.title: Where set -e Lies To You
points: errexit is famously leaky — it has ~8 documented exceptions, and every Bash veteran has been burned by at least one
Exception 1: commands in an `if` condition, `while`/`until` condition, `&&`/`||` chains, or after `!` never trigger errexit
Exception 2: any command except the last in a pipeline (that's what pipefail fixes)
Trap: `foo && bar` as the LAST line of a script or function makes the exit status the failing one — silent nonzero exit
Trap: a function called inside `if` disables errexit for the ENTIRE function body, recursively — the deadliest exception
Trap: `((count++))` returns 1 when count was 0, so arithmetic on a zero exits the script under -e; use `((count++)) || true` or `count=$((count+1))`
Trap: `let x=0` and `expr` return non-zero on a zero result for the same reason
Trap: `local x=$(failing_cmd)` masks the failure — `local` itself returns 0; declare then assign on separate lines
Same masking with `export`, `declare`, and `readonly` — always split: `local x; x=$(cmd)`
Trap: errexit is not inherited by command substitutions before bash 4.4 without `inherit_errexit`
Trap: subshells `( ... )` inherit -e but a failing subshell in a condition still gets the exception treatment
Deliberate opt-out idiom: `cmd || true` when you genuinely accept failure — make it visible, never accidental
Capture-then-check idiom: `set +e; out=$(cmd); rc=$?; set -e` for commands with meaningful non-zero exits (grep, diff)
grep returns 1 for 'no match' (not an error) and 2 for a real error — under -e, an empty grep kills your script
diff returns 1 for 'files differ'; `[ ]` returns 1 for false; both are normal, not failures
Bottom line: -e is a safety net with holes; use an ERR trap for reporting and explicit checks for anything that matters

chapters.title: Quoting, Expansion, and Word Splitting
points: Rule one: quote every expansion. `"$var"`, `"$@"`, `"$(cmd)"`, `"${arr[@]}"` — unquoted is the exception, not the default
Unquoted `$var` gets word-split on IFS then glob-expanded; `my file.txt` becomes two arguments
`"$@"` preserves each argument as a separate word; `"$*"` joins them into one string with IFS's first char; bare `$@` splits on whitespace
In `for f in "$@"` the quotes matter; `for f; do` is shorthand for the same correct behavior
`[[ ]]` does no word splitting on unquoted variables — but `[ ]` does, so `[ $x = y ]` breaks on empty or multi-word x
Prefer `[[ ]]` in Bash: safe expansion, `=~` regex, `&&`/`||` inside, and no glob surprises on the left side
But quote the RIGHT side of `==` inside `[[ ]]` or it's treated as a glob pattern: `[[ $f == "*.txt" ]]` vs `[[ $f == *.txt ]]` mean different things
Default-value expansions: `${var:-default}` (use default if unset/empty), `${var-default}` (only if unset)
`${var:?message}` errors out with your message if unset — great for required config with -u
`${var:=default}` assigns the default in place; `${var:+alt}` substitutes only when var is SET
String ops that avoid subprocesses: `${var#prefix}` `${var##prefix}` `${var%suffix}` `${var%%suffix}` `${var/old/new}` `${var//old/new}` `${#var}`
`${var,,}` lowercases, `${var^^}` uppercases (bash 4+) — no `tr` subprocess needed
Arithmetic context `$(( ))` does not need `$` on variable names and does its own expansion — never put untrusted input there (it evaluates code)
Use `$(cmd)` not backticks: nests cleanly, no backslash weirdness, and shellcheck flags backticks (SC2006)
Filenames can contain spaces, newlines, quotes, dashes, and Unicode — the only forbidden bytes are `/` and NUL

chapters.title: ShellCheck: Your Static Analyzer
points: ShellCheck is a static analyzer for shell scripts — it catches quoting bugs, useless subprocesses, and portability breaks before runtime
Run it: `shellcheck script.sh`; recurse a repo with `shellcheck $(git ls-files '*.sh')` or `find . -name '*.sh' -exec shellcheck {} +`
Severity levels: error, warning, info, style — gate CI at `--severity=warning` to start, tighten to `style` later
`-x` follows `source`d files; `-a` includes all sourced files' issues; without it, sourced definitions look undefined
Set the dialect when the shebang lies: `shellcheck -s bash` or a `# shellcheck shell=bash` directive in a fragment with no shebang
SC2086 — 'Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting' — the single most valuable check ShellCheck ships
SC2046 — unquoted `$(...)`; SC2006 — backticks; SC2148 — missing shebang; SC2164 — `cd` without `|| exit`
SC2155 — 'Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values' — the `local x=$(cmd)` trap from strict mode
SC2181 — checking `$?` instead of `if cmd; then`; SC2126 — `grep | wc -l` instead of `grep -c`
SC2115 — `rm -rf "$dir/"` where dir may be empty; the guard that saves you from `rm -rf /`
Targeted suppression with justification: `# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # word splitting is intentional here` on the line above
Repo-wide config in `.shellcheckrc`: `disable=SC1091`, `severity=warning`, `external-sources=true`
Wire it into pre-commit (`koalaman/shellcheck-precommit`) and CI so it fails the build, not just your terminal
Pair with `shfmt` for formatting (`shfmt -i 2 -ci -d`) — shellcheck for correctness, shfmt for consistency
Complement with `bats-core` for actual behavior tests: static analysis can't check your logic
Anti-pattern: blanket `# shellcheck disable=all` at the top of a file — that's deleting the smoke detector

chapters.title: Temp Files Without Tears
points: Never hardcode `/tmp/myscript.tmp` — predictable names invite symlink attacks and collide between concurrent runs
The symlink attack: attacker pre-creates `/tmp/myscript.tmp` as a symlink to `/etc/passwd`; your script writes through it as root
Correct: `tmp=$(mktemp)` for a file, `tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)` for a directory — atomic creation with mode 600 / 700
Template form: `mktemp -t myscript.XXXXXX` — the X's are required and replaced with random characters
GNU vs BSD mktemp differ on `-t`; portable form is `mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/myscript.XXXXXX"`
Always pair with cleanup: `trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT` immediately after creating it, on the very next line
Guard the removal so an unset variable can't widen it: `trap 'rm -rf -- "${tmpdir:?}"' EXIT`
Respect `$TMPDIR` — CI runners, macOS, and sandboxes point it somewhere other than /tmp
`/tmp` may be a tmpfs in RAM (size-limited) or shared between users with the sticky bit; don't stage 50 GB there
Process substitution `<(cmd)` avoids a temp file entirely: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)` — backed by /dev/fd, cleaned automatically
Here-documents and here-strings replace small temp files: `cat <<'EOF'` (quoted delimiter = no expansion) and `cmd <<< "$var"`
For secrets, prefer a pipe or `/dev/fd` over a temp file — a file on disk can be read by anyone who wins the race or reads the backup
Atomic file replacement: write to `"$target.tmp"` on the SAME filesystem, then `mv -f` — `mv` across filesystems is copy+delete, not atomic
`flock` for cross-process mutual exclusion: `exec 9>/var/lock/myscript.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1` prevents overlapping runs
Umask matters: `umask 077` before creating sensitive files so they're not world-readable

chapters.title: Traps, Cleanup, and Signals
points: `trap 'handler' SIGNAL` registers code to run on a signal or pseudo-signal — the shell's only finally block
`EXIT` fires on any exit path: normal end, `exit N`, or errexit death — the right hook for cleanup
`ERR` fires when a command fails under errexit — the right hook for reporting, not cleanup
`INT` = Ctrl-C (SIGINT, 130), `TERM` = kill (SIGTERM, 143), `HUP` = terminal closed (SIGHUP, 129)
SIGKILL (9) cannot be trapped — no cleanup runs, so design for being killed mid-write
Register the trap immediately after creating the resource, never before and never at the bottom of the file
Quote traps with single quotes so variables expand at TRAP time, not at REGISTRATION time: `trap 'rm -f "$f"' EXIT`
Make cleanup idempotent — the EXIT trap may run after a partial ERR handler; use `rm -f` and existence checks
Full error reporter: `trap 'echo "FAIL line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' ERR` with `set -E` so it fires inside functions
`$LINENO`, `$BASH_COMMAND`, `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, and `${FUNCNAME[@]}` give you a poor man's stack trace
Preserve exit code through a trap: `cleanup() { rc=$?; rm -rf "$tmp"; exit $rc; }` — otherwise the trap's own status wins
Traps are NOT inherited by functions or subshells unless you `set -E` (ERR) or `set -T` (DEBUG/RETURN)
Re-raise a signal correctly for the parent shell: `trap 'cleanup; trap - INT; kill -INT $$' INT` (exit code 128+signum)
Kill your background children on exit: `trap 'kill 0' EXIT` kills the whole process group; or track PIDs and kill them by name
Multiple pseudo-signals in one call: `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM` — but EXIT already covers most paths
`trap -p` lists current traps; `trap - EXIT` removes one

chapters.title: Idempotency: Safe to Run Twice
points: Idempotent = running the script N times leaves the same state as running it once; the property that makes retries safe
Why it matters: cron re-fires, CI reruns, humans double-click, and a network blip means you rerun a half-finished deploy
Declare the desired end state, don't perform steps: 'directory exists' not 'create directory'
`mkdir -p dir` succeeds if it exists; plain `mkdir` fails — the canonical idempotent-vs-not pair
`ln -sfn target link` replaces a symlink safely (`-n` stops it from nesting inside an existing link dir)
`rm -f` doesn't fail on a missing file; `cp -n` won't overwrite; `install -D -m 644` creates parent dirs and sets mode in one call
Guard append operations or they duplicate every run: `grep -qxF "$line" file || echo "$line" >> file`
Use `>` (truncate-and-write) over `>>` (append) when you own the whole file — writing the full file is naturally idempotent
Check-then-act has a TOCTOU race; prefer operations that are atomic or naturally repeatable over `if [ ! -e x ]`
Marker/sentinel files record completed steps: `[[ -f .step-done ]] || { do_step; touch .step-done; }`
Make it resumable: write the marker AFTER the step succeeds, and make each step independently retryable
For downloads use `curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o out.tmp && mv out.tmp out` — never leave a truncated file at the real path
`-f` in curl makes HTTP 404 a non-zero exit; without it you happily save the error page as your artifact
Idempotency vs atomicity: idempotent means safe to repeat, atomic means all-or-nothing — you often need both
Add a `--dry-run` flag that prints every mutating command instead of running it; the cheapest safety feature you can ship
This is the same principle behind Ansible/Terraform/Puppet: converge on declared state, report changed vs unchanged

chapters.title: Footgun Gallery
points: `rm -rf "$dir/"` with `$dir` empty becomes `rm -rf /` — guard with `${dir:?}` so the shell refuses to expand it
`cd "$dir"` without a check leaves you in the old directory; always `cd "$dir" || exit 1` (ShellCheck SC2164)
`for f in $(ls)` breaks on any filename with a space or newline; use a glob `for f in *` or `find -print0` with `read -d ''`
Correct null-safe loop: `while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ...; done < <(find . -print0)` — `IFS=` keeps leading spaces, `-r` keeps backslashes
Bare `read line` mangles backslashes and strips whitespace — `IFS= read -r line` is the only correct form
A `while read` loop after a pipe runs in a SUBSHELL, so variables set inside vanish; use process substitution or `shopt -s lastpipe`
`echo "$var"` breaks on values starting with `-` or containing backslashes; use `printf '%s\n' "$var"` for anything untrusted
`[ $x = y ]` with empty x is a syntax error; `[ "$x" = y ]` or `[[ $x == y ]]` is safe
`==` inside `[ ]` is a bashism; `[ ]` wants `=`. Inside `[[ ]]` both work
Integer vs string comparison: `-eq -lt -gt` are numeric; `= != < >` are lexicographic — `[ 10 -lt 9 ]` false, `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` true
Redirect order matters: `cmd > file 2>&1` merges stderr into the file, `cmd 2>&1 > file` sends stderr to the old stdout (terminal)
`a=1 b=2` on the same line as a builtin doesn't do what you expect; `var = value` with spaces is a command invocation, not an assignment
Trailing whitespace after `\` line continuation silently breaks the continuation — invisible bug, shellcheck catches it (SC1101)
`sudo cmd > /root/file` redirects as YOU, not root; use `cmd | sudo tee /root/file > /dev/null`
Windows CRLF line endings make `#!/bin/bash\r` a 'bad interpreter' error; fix with `dos2unix` or a `.gitattributes` `*.sh text eol=lf`
Never parse `ls` output; use globs, `find`, or `stat` for the fields you actually want

chapters.title: Production Script Checklist
points: Skeleton, top to bottom: shebang, `set -euo pipefail`, `IFS`, constants, `usage()`, arg parsing, `main()`, `main "$@"`
`main "$@"` at the bottom lets the whole file parse before anything runs — a partially-downloaded script can't half-execute
Resolve your own directory: `SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)` — never assume the caller's cwd
Parse flags with a `while getopts` loop or a `case` over `$@`; always support `-h/--help` and print usage to stdout on request, stderr on error
Validate inputs early and loudly: required args, file existence, tool availability via `command -v jq >/dev/null || die 'need jq'`
Log to stderr, data to stdout — so `script.sh | jq` works and logs still reach the human
`die() { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }` — one helper, used everywhere, consistent exit path
Meaningful exit codes: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 usage error; reserve 64-78 for sysexits.h conventions if you care
Never put secrets in argv (visible in `ps`), in the script, or in a temp file — read from env, a file descriptor, or a secrets manager
Beware `set -x` leaking secrets into CI logs; disable tracing around credential handling
Quote every variable, use `--` before user-supplied paths (`rm -- "$f"`) so a leading dash isn't read as a flag
Pin your dependencies and check versions; a script that works on GNU coreutils may break on BSD/macOS (`sed -i`, `date`, `readlink -f`)
Test with bats-core, run shellcheck + shfmt in CI, and dry-run against a scratch environment before production
The five-line safety core to memorize: `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, `set -euo pipefail`, `IFS=$'\n\t'`, `trap cleanup EXIT`, `tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)`
Final rule: a Bash script that can't fail loudly, can't be run twice, and can't be read by the next person is a production incident waiting for a date
